items.title: Weekly Update 531: Optimizely. Script Dependencies & Third Parties
items.summary: "You can't outsource accountability". But it feels like that's what's happening when a disclosure notice refers to "an incident being at a third party", as though somehow that makes it better. It feels like the intent is to deflect responsibility , but ultimately, accountability remains with the party we entrusted our data to in the first place. It's also ultimately them who needs to decide whether to disclose the incident, so in the case of Optimizely this week, even though it's clearly their fault, it's up to the likes of Norwegian Airlines to decide whether they're contacting impacted individuals. And then, in their case, they haven't named the third party anyway! Strange times, I reckon.

items.title: OpenRouter Users’ Private AI Chats Possibly Exposed Via Compromised Third-Party Providers
items.summary: OpenRouter has removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after researchers found evidence that some providers had been compromised or had failed to follow their data policies. In its November 22 incident notice , OpenRouter said it notified all potentially affected customers. The findings did not show a breach of OpenRouter itself, and the company did not say how many users or conversations may have been exposed. OpenRouter AI Chat Leaks OpenRouter gives customers a single API for accessing AI models hosted by different providers. But the company that first receives a request may not be the only one that handles it. If a provider forwards the request to another service, that service can also see the prompt. As Cyber Security News explained in its comparison of AI privacy gateways , routing requests and keeping them confidential are separate tasks. In its research report , Dragos said it sent nearly two million test prompts between July and November 2026. The prompts contained unique links and test credentials known as canary tokens. When a link was opened, or a credential was used, researchers could trace it to the original request. Dragos found evidence of compromises at three hosting providers. Some test requests were copied even though the model rejected them before processing. The researchers also saw signs that some requests marked for Zero Data Retention, a policy that says prompts and replies should not be stored, were kept or forwarded. In one case, a test link sent to a U.S. provider surfaced in a company chat in China 24 days later. What OpenRouter Users Should Check OpenRouter’s provider disclosures list notices from Novita, Phala, and Together. The company said it removed some endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility as a precaution, so the 125 removals do not represent 125 confirmed breaches. It is checking whether providers forward requests or replies to other companies and plans to verify endpoints before restoring their eligibility. Customers who received a notice should review what they sent through the affected provider. If prompts contained passwords or API keys, revoke or rotate them and check access logs for unusual activity. Earlier Cyber Security News reporting on exposed Clawdbot gateways showed why chat histories and credentials need to be reviewed together. For future requests, restrict sensitive workloads to approved providers and keep secrets out of prompts rather than relying on retention settings alone. items.title: Hackers Could Execute Commands on WordPress, Email and Print Servers Through Upload2Shell Flaw
items.summary: A flaw in Ghostscript let researchers run commands on WordPress, Roundcube webmail, and Linux print servers through routine file processing. The vulnerability, dubbed Upload2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-125396, affects upstream Ghostscript releases before 10.08.0. It sits in the software’s Type 1 font loader, but the affected servers did not need to expose Ghostscript directly. Their own preview, thumbnail, and print features delivered files to it. The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and lists a local attack vector. That describes the flaw at the interpreter level, not how a document arrives there. In research published on November 17, Paulos Yibelo and pwn.ai showed that network-facing services could pass remotely supplied files to the vulnerable code. The report describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks in the wild. Upload2Shell Bypassed Ghostscript’s Sandbox Ghostscript renders PDFs and PostScript documents. PostScript is a programming language for describing pages, so rendering a file means running instructions from it. Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode is meant to limit what those instructions can access. Upload2Shell undermined those limits through a use-after-free, a memory flaw in which software keeps a reference to data after releasing the memory that held it. The font loader failed to check the type of data it received before an operation that could raise an error. That error exposed a protected write that document code was not supposed to control. Researchers used the resulting memory flaw to alter Ghostscript’s security checks while -dSAFER was still enabled. The test commands ran with the renderer’s permissions, not automatically as root. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of a separate Ghostscript PDF flaw , those permissions help determine what an attacker can reach after gaining code execution. WordPress, Roundcube and CUPS were Exposed On WordPress, the researchers reached Ghostscript through the media preview process on a site using Imagick and ImageMagick. The WordPress advisory tracks the core upload issue separately as CVE-2026-65640. It requires media upload privileges, which Authors and higher roles have by default. As covered in our WordPress Imagick vulnerability report , WordPress fixed that route in 7.0.4 and backported the fix, including to 6.9.7. The researchers also found that certain public upload features in Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor reached the renderer without a login in the configurations tested. On Roundcube 1.7.2, the sender needed no webmail account. The recipient had to view the message, but did not have to click or download the attachment. Roundcube’s server generated a thumbnail and passed the attachment through ImageMagick to Ghostscript. The test depended on an ImageMagick policy that allowed the handoff. The command ran as www-data , the web service account, rather than on the recipient’s device. The print server required no action from a recipient. On Debian 13, a shared CUPS queue accepted network print jobs without credentials and sent the test document to Ghostscript for conversion. The researchers confirmed command execution by writing a marker file as lp , the print service account. Requiring authentication blocked anonymous submission in the test, but did not repair the underlying flaw. These were three ways to reach the same vulnerable renderer, not three separate flaws in Ghostscript. Artifex fixed the underlying flaw in Ghostscript 10.08.0. Linux distributions can apply the same fix to an older release, so the upstream version number alone is not enough to judge exposure. Debian 13, for example, first shipped the fix in 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u2 . Administrators should check their vendor’s package status for CVE-2026-125396 and verify the copy used by each service. Updating the host does not replace Ghostscript inside an existing container or application bundle. WordPress operators should apply both the core and renderer updates and review public forms that send uploads into the Media Library. If patching must wait, suspend automatic previews for untrusted files where practical. On print servers, require authentication for shared queues and restrict network access to them. Keep renderers isolated and give their service accounts only the access they need. The key check comes after a file is accepted. Storing a file did not start Ghostscript in the researchers’ tests. Rendering it did. Trace the worker that actually makes the preview, thumbnail or print output, then verify that worker uses the patched package. The print server required no action from a recipient. On Debian 13, a shared CUPS queue accepted network print jobs without credentials and sent the test document to Ghostscript for conversion. The researchers confirmed command execution by writing a marker file as lp, the print service account.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Microsoft Entra Connect Health Flaw to Access Admin Emails and Organization Data
items.summary: Attackers exploited a flaw in Microsoft Entra Connect Health to read administrator and technical contact email addresses, along with configuration data from affected organizations. A Microsoft customer notice shared on Reddit describes read-only access to those records, not access to inboxes or email messages. Microsoft fixed the flaw in its cloud service on November 19, 2026, and said customers do not need to install a patch. Microsoft said the vulnerability was introduced on July 23 and detected on November 9. Investigators reviewed service logs for unauthorized requests and concluded on November 20 that attackers had read tenant data. The flaw could also have allowed changes to monitoring settings, but Microsoft found none. The notice does not say when the unauthorized access began, who was behind it, or how many organizations were affected. Entra Connect Health Flaw Exposed Microsoft Entra Connect Health lets IT teams view alerts, performance data, and directory sync errors for identity systems running on their own servers. The flaw was in the cloud monitoring service’s API. Unlike a separate Entra ID flaw involving Global Administrator privileges , this incident involved confirmed reads of tenant records, with no reported takeover of administrator accounts through the flaw. The records included each affected tenant’s ID, display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope, and Entra license tier. They also showed whether directory sync was enabled, when it last ran, and whether the organization had set up Connect Health. The API still returned an expired certificate once used to register monitoring agents with an internal Microsoft service shut down in late 2024. Microsoft said the flaw did not expose passwords, password hashes, sign-in tokens, valid cryptographic keys, Azure subscription details, or details about how local Active Directory servers were arranged. The cloud fix stopped further access through the flaw, but it cannot take back the contact details already exposed. Knowing who administers a tenant and which domain it uses could make a fake support message more convincing. Previous Microsoft 365 phishing campaigns show why unexpected sign-in requests deserve scrutiny. The notice did not report any phishing linked to this incident. Microsoft advised organizations to alert their IT and security teams, confirm their technical contact details, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for privileged accounts. Where available, teams should use Privileged Identity Management to grant admin access only when needed. They should also check Connect Health settings and review Entra audit and sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for unexpected changes or unusual administrator activity. Administrators should open the Azure portal directly and check the security advisory in Azure Service Health to confirm whether it lists their tenant. The notice also points to Microsoft’s read-only GetTenant PowerShell script, which shows the types of records the API could have returned. It reports current values, so it cannot reconstruct what attackers saw or tell an organization which specific records were read. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks?
